strengths: The connection between interventionist explanation and causal discovery over interpretable features has a clear audience in explainable ML and algorithm auditing. Applying established FCI machinery can be a worthwhile contribution without introducing a new algorithm.

Using PAGs to accommodate omitted features and distinguish definite ancestry, possible ancestry, and confounding is well motivated. The background constraint that predictions cannot cause input attributes is also sensible.

The synthetic example deliberately omits a relevant feature, directly illustrating the motivation for handling latent confounding. The two annotated image applications make the proposed workflow concrete.
The manuscript clearly explains its focus on explanations of population-level behavior and acknowledges limitations involving annotations, background knowledge, and validation.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the causal statements in Section IV. The stated graph contains H ← U1 → V → Y, so H is not marginally independent of Y. Conditioning only on C also leaves R ← H ← U1 → V → Y open, contradicting the claimed conditional independence. Furthermore, Fig. 4(b) permits H → V → Ŷ, so it cannot establish that interventions on H would have no effect. The proposed interpretation procedure must distinguish nonadjacency from absence of possible ancestry when declaring features noncausal.

Necessary: Strengthen the link between the assumed model and the predictor being explained. In Section III, an observational approximation Ŷ ≈ g(Ẑ, ε) does not itself establish that interventions on semantic image attributes obey that structural model. State the intervention-preservation assumption explicitly and delimit the applicability of FCI’s guarantees. In Section IV, 81% classification accuracy does not establish that the trained CNN shares the label generator’s causal dependencies. Controlled interventions on the simulated shapes could validate this claim; otherwise, narrow the example’s conclusions.

Necessary: Address selection bias in the X-ray experiment. Section V-A selects controls with 'no findings,' constraining the explanatory disease labels in controls and producing a pneumonia-versus-no-findings sample. Such selection can alter the dependencies used by FCI, whereas Section II dismisses selection bias as irrelevant. Account for this sampling mechanism or narrow the interpretation. Stable associations with general abnormality do not establish that the classifier has learned pneumonia-specific causal features.

Necessary: Establish the reliability of the conditional-independence tests and preserve orientation uncertainty in the results. With 239 X-rays and multivalued bird attributes, conditional chi-square tests can involve sparse contingency tables; relevant diagnostics are missing. Bootstrapping does not resolve invalid test calibration. Figure 5 also pools directed and circle-arrow edges, although a stable circle-arrow edge remains compatible with pure confounding. Report these frequencies separately, assess sensitivity to testing and conditioning-set restrictions, and avoid treating low adjacency stability as evidence of causal irrelevance.

Necessary for reproducibility: Specify which observations supplied predictions for graph learning, whether those predictions were out of sample, and how repeated patients were handled in splitting and bootstrapping. Supply the grouping and attribute specifications referenced as supplementary material but absent from the provided manuscript. Also reconcile the reported 74.55% accuracy with a stated test set of 50 images.

Optional: An associational explanation using the same semantic attributes would help isolate the contribution of causal discovery from the contribution of annotations. The current LIME/SHAP illustrations compare both different representations and different explanation scopes. Clearer graph layouts and explicit class labels in the SHAP panels would also improve usability.
